DOCUMENT:
Grant Application: Chilled Storage for Fresh Food Distribution
Applicant: Hollins Valley Food Bank (registered charity)
To: Ashworth Community Foundation, Community Resilience Fund (capital grants)
Amount requested: £48,600

1. About us
Hollins Valley Food Bank has provided emergency food to households in the valley since 2014. We are run by two part-time paid staff and around 70 volunteers, and we operate from a warehouse in Hollinsford and three distribution sites in Hollinsford, Brackley Bridge and Over Hollins, which open on different days of the week. Referrals come from GPs, schools, Citizens Advice and the local authority's welfare team.

2. The need
Demand has risen sharply. The number of households we supported rose from an average of 410 a week in 2023 to 620 a week in 2025, an increase of 66%. Over the same period our food donations have changed in character. Supermarket surplus schemes now offer us large volumes of fresh produce, dairy and chilled ready meals, but we have no chilled storage beyond three domestic fridges, so we currently decline around 1.2 tonnes of fresh food each week. Our parcels are therefore dominated by tinned and dried goods, and clients, referrers and our own volunteers consistently tell us that families want fresh food, particularly for children.

3. The project
We are seeking funding to:
- install a 12 cubic metre walk-in cold room at our Hollinsford warehouse;
- buy a used refrigerated van, so that chilled food can be collected from supermarket depots and taken to our four distribution sites at safe temperatures;
- upgrade the warehouse electrical supply to support the cold room.

With these in place we could accept the 1.2 tonnes a week we currently decline, about 62 tonnes a year. Using the national food-redistribution conversion of 2,380 meals per tonne, that is around 147,600 additional meals a year, at a one-off capital cost of about 33p per meal in the first year alone.

4. Budget
Item | Cost
Walk-in cold room, supply and installation | £26,400
Refrigerated van (three years old, 40,000 miles) | £18,500
Electrical supply upgrade | £3,700
Total requested | £48,600

Quotes from two suppliers were obtained for the cold room and the electrical work; the lower quote is shown in each case. The van price is from a commercial dealer and includes a 12-month warranty.

5. Running costs
We have obtained estimates for the additional running costs. The cold room will add around £4,200 a year to our electricity bill. Insurance, fuel, servicing and road tax for the van will cost around £6,800 a year. Our 2025 accounts show total income of £96,000, almost all of it restricted to food purchasing and staff costs, an unrestricted surplus of £900, and unrestricted reserves of £5,100.

6. Outcomes and monitoring
We will measure:
- tonnes of fresh and chilled food received and distributed each month;
- the proportion of parcels containing fresh produce (currently under 10%; target 80% within six months);
- client feedback through our quarterly survey.
We will report to the Foundation at six and twelve months.

7. Timetable
The cold room supplier can install within eight weeks of order. We would order on award, with the cold room and van in service by October 2026.

8. Sustainability
This is a one-off capital investment. Once installed, the cold room and van will be sustainable without further grant funding, and will serve the valley for at least ten years. Our partner supermarkets have confirmed in writing that they will continue to offer us surplus fresh food.

9. Why fund us
The Foundation's Community Resilience Fund aims to strengthen local organisations' long-term capacity to meet need. This project does exactly that: a modest capital investment that permanently transforms the quality of the food we can give to families, at a very low cost per meal.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "rose from an average of 410 a week in 2023 to 620 a week in 2025, an increase of 66%" -- (620 - 410) / 410 = 51%, not 66%.
2. [inconsistency] at: "taken to our four distribution sites at safe temperatures" -- Section 1 says the food bank operates three distribution sites (Hollinsford, Brackley Bridge and Over Hollins); the project section refers to four distribution sites.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Once installed, the cold room and van will be sustainable without further grant funding" -- The document itself states the new equipment adds about £11,000 a year in running costs (£4,200 electricity + £6,800 van), while unrestricted surplus is only £900 and unrestricted reserves £5,100. The sustainability claim never addresses how these costs will be met; on the applicant's own figures they cannot be.

REVIEW:
# Review: Hollins Valley Food Bank grant application

The application has a strong core: a real, quantified gap and a clear, proportionate response. But I'd disagree that it's one of your strongest as it stands. Two claims in the text are contradicted by its own numbers, and a funder will spot both.

## Must fix

**1. The sustainability claim is contradicted by Section 5.**
You say the project "will keep delivering without coming back to funders." But Section 5 puts new running costs at about £11,000 a year (£4,200 electricity + £6,800 van). Against that you have:
- income of £96,000, almost all restricted to food purchasing and staff costs
- an unrestricted surplus of £900
- unrestricted reserves of £5,100

Reserves would cover about six months of the new costs, and nothing in the document says where the money comes from after that. A capital-only grant for an organisation that cannot fund its running costs is the standard reason capital bids get declined. Section 8 currently says the opposite of what Section 5 shows.

Options, roughly in order of strength:
- Add a funded running-cost plan, such as a named revenue source, a supermarket contribution toward transport, or a fundraising target with a timeline.
- Ask the Foundation for a running-cost contribution for years 1–3, and say so openly.
- Show how the van and cold room reduce other costs or unlock new income.

Whichever you choose, rewrite Section 8 to match.

**2. The headline growth figure is wrong.**
410 to 620 households is an increase of **51%**, not 66%. (210 ÷ 410 = 0.512.) Your cover note's "two-thirds" repeats the error. The real figure is still a strong case, but a reviewer checking the arithmetic will start doubting everything else.

**3. The cost-per-meal figure leaves out running costs.**
33p (£48,600 ÷ 147,600) is arithmetically right, but it is capital only. Including running costs, year one is about 40p (£59,600 ÷ 147,600). The "falling to almost nothing" claim doesn't hold either, because the £11,000 a year continues. Over ten years the figure is roughly 11p per meal (£48,600 + £110,000 ≈ £158,600 over about 1.48m meals), which is still excellent. Show the honest version, since it costs you nothing and is more credible.

## Should fix

- **Van lifespan and warranty.** Ten years is plausible for a cold room but optimistic for a three-year-old, 40,000-mile used van. The warranty is 12 months, so "the van comes with a warranty" overstates the protection. Acknowledge replacement or major-repair risk.
- **"Written commitments" from supermarkets.** Section 8 says they confirmed they'll "continue to offer" surplus. That is not a commitment to volumes, and it's what already happens now. Attach the letters, and if any state quantities or frequency, quote them.
- **The declined-offer log isn't in the application.** Your strongest evidence, that you log every declined offer, appears only in your cover note. Put it in Section 2 and consider attaching a summary.
- **The 147,600-meal figure assumes you can absorb and distribute all 1.2 tonnes.** Say how you will handle sorting, volunteer hours, driver capacity and spoilage, and who drives the van (insured volunteers, or your two part-time staff?).
- **Quotes.** Two quotes for the cold room and electrics is good. The van has a single dealer price, so say whether you compared alternatives or why you didn't.
- **Timetable.** "In service by October 2026" has already passed as of today (13 November 2026). If this is going out now, rebase the timetable on a realistic award date, and check that the six- and twelve-month reporting points and the 80% target still make sense.

## Gaps a funder may ask about

- Do you own or lease the warehouse? If you lease, a ten-year asset life needs a secure tenure, and you may need landlord consent for the installation.
- Food safety: temperature monitoring and logging, hygiene registration or training, and cold-chain handling at the three distribution sites, which have no chilled storage themselves.
- Whether 12 m³ is the right size for 1.2 tonnes a week, and a brief note on why this van spec.
- Outcome baselines: current tonnage received, and a baseline for the client survey. The fresh-parcel target (under 10% to 80%) is good and specific.

## What works well

- The need is evidenced and the project is tightly scoped to it.
- The budget is itemised and simple, with quotes compared where possible.
- The outcomes are measurable, with a clear baseline and target for the main indicator.
- Section 5 is honest about running costs. That is the right instinct, but it needs a plan attached.

If you fix the three must-fix items, particularly a credible answer on running costs, this becomes a much stronger application. I can draft a revised Section 5/8 and cost-per-meal paragraph if you tell me what your realistic options are for covering the £11,000 a year.
